questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Assumptions hidden in the logistic model
questions.learningObjective: Identify the assumptions embedded in the logistic growth equation
questions.stem: A dashboard note on the logistic model states that a population on a crowded island is modelled by dN over dt equals r N times one minus N over K. Which assumption is buried inside that equation?

options.text: The population is open, so arrivals and departures continue throughout the year.
options.misconception: assumes immigration and emigration continue at a constant rate

options.text: The intrinsic rate r changes as the population approaches carrying capacity.
options.misconception: assumes the per-capita growth rate varies with density

options.text: The population is closed, and both r and K stay constant over the modelled period.
Carrying capacity is reached at once, so the model predicts a fixed population throughout.
options.misconception: treats carrying capacity as the population from the start

questions.explanation: The equation has no terms for immigration or emigration, so it assumes a closed population with constant r and K. Carrying capacity is a limit approached over time, not a state reached at once.
questions.hint: Look for what the equation leaves out.

questions.stem: The surveillance panel shows five survey nights, each with a detection probability of 0.4 when the target species is present. What is the probability of missing it across all five nights?

questions.hint: Raise the nightly miss probability to the fifth power.

options.misconception: assumes any damage at all justifies control spending

options.text: Treatment should wait, because the loss of 240 per hectare is below the 300 cost.
The field has passed the threshold, because twenty pests per hectare is already high.

questions.topic: Break-even density for a pest treatment
questions.learningObjective: Plan the calculation of a break-even pest density
questions.stem: The treatment panel asks at what pest density a treatment stops paying for itself. Describe how that break-even density should be worked out from the dashboard data.

answer.exemplar: For each candidate density the analyst multiplies the estimated pest density by the loss caused per pest to obtain the expected damage per hectare, then compares that figure with the treatment cost per hectare. The break-even density is the density at which the two are equal, found by solving the damage equation, and the answer is reported with a sensitivity check showing how much it shifts if the loss per pest estimate changes.

questions.explanation: Equating expected damage with control cost defines the break-even point, and the sensitivity check shows how firm the answer is. Without that check a single estimate could make the programme look worthwhile when it is not.
questions.hint: Set damage equal to cost and solve for density.

questions.stem: A fitted logistic curve on the dashboard assumes a weed population on a disturbed plot rises from 200 to 800 and then levels off near 1000. Which reading of the curve is valid?

options.misconception: ignores the flattening that marks the ceiling

options.text: The population has already reached its carrying capacity of 1000 individuals.
options.misconception: reads the asymptote as an already attained population

options.text: The population is approaching a ceiling near 1000 but has not reached it yet.
The population can only grow by 200 more, because that was the first step.
options.misconception: assumes growth repeats the first observed increment

questions.explanation: The logistic population approaches K asymptotically, so at 800 it is still below the ceiling of 1000 and keeps growing slowly. Reaching K would mean growth stops, which this curve has not yet shown.
questions.hint: An asymptote is approached, never reached.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Eradication declared on the last sighting
questions.learningObjective: Design a survey protocol that can justify an eradication claim
questions.stem: To confirm that an invasive species is truly gone, the team needs a defensible survey protocol. Outline the steps that would justify declaring eradication.

answer.exemplar: Survey a set of sites where the species was last confirmed, repeat the survey several times across a full seasonal cycle, and record the hours of searching effort so that detection probability can be estimated from the known detections. Combine this with trapping and monitoring records from the same period, and only declare eradication when the probability of missing the species after all that searching is small enough for the decision being made.

questions.explanation: An eradication claim must rest on search effort and the resulting chance of missing the species, not on the absence of sightings alone. Repeating the survey across a full cycle covers seasonal refuges where the species may persist.
questions.hint: Report search effort and the residual chance of missing it.

options.misconception: believes herd immunity requires universal individual immunity

options.text: Herd immunity matters only for diseases that cannot be caught twice.
options.misconception: limits herd immunity to diseases without reinfection

options.misconception: treats herd immunity as a guarantee of no transmission

questions.explanation: Herd immunity is a population effect: enough immune people stop transmission sustaining itself, so cases decline rather than vanish. It needs no universal immunity, and its protection scales with coverage.
questions.hint: It is a population effect, not a guarantee.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Threshold for herd immunity
questions.learningObjective: Plan the estimation of a basic reproduction number
questions.stem: To find the herd immunity threshold for a district, the analyst must estimate the basic reproduction number. Describe how that estimate should be made from the dashboard data.

answer.exemplar: The analyst takes the number of secondary cases generated by each case during the early phase of an outbreak, when most of the population is still susceptible, using the case line list rather than later counts where immunity has built up. The mean of those case counts gives R zero, the threshold fraction is one minus one over R zero, and the district population is multiplied by that fraction to give the number of people who must be immune.

questions.explanation: R zero must be measured early while the susceptible pool is nearly intact, otherwise immunity built up during the outbreak biases it downwards. The threshold then follows directly from that estimate.
questions.hint: Measure early, while most people are still susceptible.

questions.learningObjective: Design a study that separates density from total host numbers
questions.stem: To estimate how transmission responds to host density, the team needs a design that separates density from total numbers. Describe the design the analyst should use.

answer.exemplar: The team should set up villages or wards that differ in crowding while keeping the total number of hosts as similar as possible, and in a second series vary the total number of hosts in a village while keeping crowding fixed. questions.explanation: Two series vary crowding and total numbers independently, so only then can their effects be separated. Converting to cases per host per day gives a rate that can be compared directly between groups.

answer.exemplar: The team should pair comparable neighbourhoods, remove or treat breeding sites in one member of each pair and leave the other unchanged, and monitor adult mosquito density with the same trap effort at the same times in both. questions.explanation: Paired treated and untreated areas control for weather and other background effects, and replication across several pairs shows the pattern is general. Matching trap effort keeps the measurement itself comparable.

questions.topic: Density-dependent transmission
questions.learningObjective: Plan the measurement of a per-capita transmission rate
questions.stem: To measure how host density changes the rate of infection, the analyst needs a sampling and measurement plan. Describe how the rate should be measured.

answer.exemplar: For each study village the team should record the number of hosts, the number of new cases over a fixed follow-up period, and the effort spent finding cases so that ascertainment stays comparable. The rate is then computed as cases divided by hosts divided by time, and the villages are grouped by density so the relationship between crowding and per host rate can be plotted and tested rather than assumed.

questions.explanation: A per host rate with a recorded follow-up period and comparable case-finding effort makes villages comparable, and grouping by density exposes the relationship. Without effort recorded, differences in case finding could masquerade as density effects.
questions.hint: Standardise effort and divide by hosts and time.
